content: Finance transcription turns spoken financial content into written text: earnings calls, analyst Q&A, investor days, client reviews, budget and board meetings, and market podcasts. Analysts search it, advisers keep it with their meeting notes, and investor relations teams publish or archive it.

Typing up one hour of audio by hand takes about four hours. TranscriptX turns the recording into text in seconds and keeps a timestamp on each paragraph, so you spend your time checking the numbers and using the transcript instead of typing it.

sections.h2: How to Transcribe a Financial Call

steps.content: Upload the audio or video file from your device, Google Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive, such as an earnings call replay or a Zoom or Teams recording. If the call is on YouTube, paste the link. For a meeting in the room, press Record.
TranscriptX detects the language and writes out the call as punctuated paragraphs, each with a timestamp.

steps.h3: Check the figures against the audio
steps.content: Play the recording beside the text, correct numbers, names and tickers with Edit, and note key figures and follow-ups in the Notes tab.
Copy the transcript into a research note or email, or download it as DOCX, PDF or TXT for reports and records.

content: There is nothing to install. Open this page in your browser on a computer or phone, add the recording, and the transcript appears on the same page.

Most financial audio arrives as a file: a webcast replay from an investor relations page, a meeting recording from Zoom, Teams or Meet, or a voice memo after a client call. Both audio and video files work. If the call or market update is already online as a video, paste the link instead of downloading it first.
You can try financial audio transcription free, without an account. If you transcribe calls every week, see the Pro plan.

sections.h2: Check the Numbers Before You Quote
intro: In a financial transcript, one wrong digit changes the meaning. Speech recognition handles everyday language well; check the parts that sound alike or depend on context:

items.content: "Fifteen" and "fifty", "thirteen" and "thirty": 15% growth is not 50%.
"Million" and "billion" are short words on a fast call. Check them against the press release or slides.
Up 40 basis points is not up 40%. Keep the unit the speaker used.
Ranges like "1.20 to 1.30" and periods like Q3 FY26 are easy to blur. Confirm both.
Company and analyst names, tickers, and words like "not" or "no longer" deserve a second listen.

sections.h2: Speaker Labels for Executives and Analysts
content: Earnings calls and client meetings have several voices: the CEO, the CFO, investor relations, analysts, advisers and clients. On the Pro plan, TranscriptX labels speakers automatically, so you can see who gave the guidance and who asked the question.

Rename each label to the person's role or name during your review. On the Free plan, you get timestamped paragraphs without speaker names, which works well for a single presenter or a two-person call.

sections.h2: Financial Transcription for Webinars and Videos
content: Investor webinars, results videos and market updates reach more people with subtitles. Download the transcript as SRT or VTT and upload it to your video platform or webinar replay.
The same transcript works as a text version of the video for your investor relations page, a newsletter or a blog post.

items.content: Seconds to minutes, free to try. A solid draft on clear audio that you review before quoting. Best for earnings calls, research, client and team meetings.

Paid per audio minute and slower, but reviewed by a person. Some offer verified or certified transcripts for legal disputes, regulatory filings or formal records.

content: Financial calls often hold client details or non-public information. Check your firm's policy on which tools may handle them, and get consent before recording a client meeting.

Uploaded files are deleted automatically, and your recordings and transcripts are not used to train AI models. You can delete a single transcript, or all your data, at any time from your account. See the Privacy Policy for details.

items.q: How do I transcribe an earnings call?
items.a: Download the replay from the company's investor relations page and upload it, or paste the link if the call is on YouTube. Then check the figures against the press release before you quote them.
You can try TranscriptX free, without an account. Speaker labels and noise reduction are on the Pro plan.

items.q: How accurate is AI transcription for financial calls?
items.a: Clear recordings come back as a solid draft. Always check numbers, names and tickers against the audio before you publish or rely on them.

items.q: How long does it take to transcribe an earnings call?
items.a: A few minutes of audio comes back in seconds, and a full call takes a little longer. Plan extra time to check the figures.

items.q: Can I fix a transcript that has errors?
items.a: Yes. Use Edit to correct any word, number or name, playing the recording beside the text as you go.

items.q: Can I transcribe a Zoom or Teams client meeting?
items.a: Yes. Upload the recording file afterwards. TranscriptX doesn't join calls itself.

items.q: Can I use it for regulatory or legal records?
items.a: Use it for drafts, notes and searching the recording. When a verified or certified transcript is required, use a human transcription service and follow your firm's rules.
